To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
NFP is an important form of birth control, that health-care professionals are not adequately trained in it, and that they would use it if they were.

1) the extant English language scientific literature contains limited information on the training in NFP received by medical and nursing students; and 2) the literature suggests that many physicians and nurses would be willing to provide NFP to their patients if they had better knowledge of the methods and were more adequately trained in NFP.

NFP is an underutilised form of contraception; the reasons for this are unknown; it is possible that one of the reasons is a lack of knowledge about the methods among nurses and doctors; the extent to which NFP is taught in undergraduate and graduate medical and nursing programs is not known; there is little data to indicate whether NFP is used by nurses or physicians; there are no data that indicate whether or not physicians and nurses would use NFP if they knew more about it.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a number of issues: (a) the extent and quality of education in NFP in nursing and medical schools; (b) the attitudes of health care professionals toward NFP; (c) the extent to which NFP is offered by health care providers; and (d) the extent to, and ways in which, health care professionals are willing to offer NFP to their patients.

the current state of NFP training and practice in the medical and nursing professions is not optimal.

there is a clear need for more research on the subject, including on the efficacy of different NFP methods.
